answer:
The ideal numbers show the Mott effect clearly. The device numbers cannot show it, because garnet:mock returns random counts.

What I ran. I built the 2-site Hubbard model on 4 qubits. The qubits are site 1 up, site 1 down, site 2 up and site 2 down. For each U, I ran a variational search (VQE) on a noiseless simulator. The circuit keeps the electron count fixed. It uses Givens rotations for each spin, then on-site interaction steps and hopping steps, repeated in 2 layers with 8 parameters. A first version of the circuit kept the complex phases wrong and stopped at half the true energy. I fixed that before submitting. The final energies match the exact formula E = U/2 - sqrt(U^2/4 + 4) to 6 digits. They are -2.000 at U=0, -1.236 at U=2, -0.828 at U=4 and -0.472 at U=8, in units of t. I then sent the 4 optimized circuits as one job of 1000 shots each to IQM's free Garnet test device, garnet:mock. The job ID is 01a160a9-212c-71ab-9e48-c662712c0a50. The test device cost 0 credits.

What the numbers show. Double occupancy is the chance that one site holds both an up and a down electron. I simulated the exact circuits the server received, without noise. That gives 0.250 at U=0, 0.138 at U=2, 0.073 at U=4 and 0.026 at U=8. At U=0 the electrons ignore each other. Then a site is doubly occupied 25% of the time, which is pure chance. As the repulsion U grows, the electrons stop sharing a site. At U=8 they almost always sit one per site. The energy also rises toward 0. The electrons give up most of the energy they gain by hopping, because a hop would put two of them on one site.

The device values are 0.353, 0.358, 0.401 and 0.373. They do not follow U. The test device does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bitstrings, so these numbers only show that the job ran. To see the trend in device data, you would run the same 4 circuits on the real Garnet machine, which costs credits. Each circuit has 48 to 62 two-qubit gates, so noise there would blur the result.

What this says about La2CuO4. Each copper atom in the crystal gives about one electron to the conducting band, so the band is half full. Simple band theory says a half-full band conducts, and the U=0 case shows the reason. Electrons move freely and pile up on sites by chance. In the real crystal, the repulsion on a copper site is several times larger than the hopping energy. That case is like U=8 here. A moving electron would have to land on a copper atom that already holds an electron, and that costs energy U. So the electrons stay put, one per copper atom, and the crystal is an insulator. The leftover hopping lets neighboring spins lower their energy by pointing in opposite directions. That is why La2CuO4 is also an antiferromagnet. Superconductivity appears when chemists remove some of these electrons, which is called doping. Two sites are only a toy version of this. The model shows the cause of the Mott state, but it cannot show a true phase transition.
